opus-5.5.text:
Ha, well, it's the first thing people say when they walk in, so I can't take full credit for it. You come through the door expecting a normal office, and instead there's a whole floor that looks like a mix between an apartment, a warehouse, and a playground. There's a kitchen with real counters and dishes in the sink, a living room with couches and toys on the floor, stairs, different kinds of flooring, doors that stick a little. And robots are moving through all of it: picking things up, bumping into things, trying again.

What makes it feel like Willy Wonka is that it's a place built for wonder, but it's also a factory. Everything in there exists to produce something, which is data and learning. Every cup that gets knocked over or towel that gets folded badly teaches the system something. So you get this strange, delightful mix of whimsy and very serious engineering. Adults walk in and act like kids again. They want to touch everything, they ask a hundred questions, they try to trip up the robot.

There's a practical reason we built it that way, too. The real world is messy, and if you only test robots in clean, controlled lab conditions, you end up with robots that only work in clean, controlled labs. We wanted an environment that's deliberately a little chaotic and full of surprises, because that's what homes and workplaces actually look like. So it's fun, yes, but the fun is kind of the point. The weirdness is what makes the robots better.

r001.rationale: It describes a deliberately varied, messy office-like environment, but does not say the robots are tested in exact replicas of customers’ work cells.

r002.rationale: It mentions robots moving, picking things up, and retrying, but does not identify prolonged standing without corrective movements as an ability being tested.

fable-5.1.text:
Ha, well, you walk in and the first thing you notice is that it doesn't look like an office. There are robots everywhere, and they're all doing different things. In one corner you've got a humanoid trying to fold laundry, badly, and over and over again. Next to it there's a robot arm picking things out of bins and dropping them, and someone's standing there with a tablet watching it fail and taking notes like it's the most fascinating thing in the world. There's a mock kitchen, a mock warehouse aisle, a little apartment setup with a couch and a fridge.

And it changes constantly. You come in on a Tuesday and there's a whole new station that didn't exist on Friday, because somebody had an idea over the weekend and just built it. So it has that feeling of, "What's behind this door?" Every room is a different experiment.

The "for adults" part is that everyone there is deeply serious about it. These are engineers who have spent years on this, and they're obsessive about the details, like how the gripper handles a slightly deformed cardboard box. But at the same time, you can't help grinning. You see a robot finally get the fold right after three hundred attempts and the whole team cheers. It's playful and rigorous at the same time, and that combination is rare. Most workplaces are one or the other.

I also think it's a bit of a candy store in the sense that it's dangerous to let visitors loose in there. Everybody wants to touch the robots, give them a task, see what they'll do. We've had to put up a lot of tape on the floor.

r001.rationale: It mentions mock settings such as a kitchen, warehouse aisle, and apartment, but does not describe exact replicas of customers’ work cells.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention testing robots’ ability to stand for prolonged periods without corrective movements.

astra-6.text: It’s that feeling of walking into a place where there’s always something unexpected happening. We’ve got robots moving around, people trying things, testing what works and figuring out what doesn’t. For someone who loves technology, that’s a playground. You get to take an idea and watch it do something in the physical world. That’s what I mean by “Willy Wonka for adults”—that sense of curiosity and possibility.

sol-6.1.text: It’s that sense of walking into a place where there’s something surprising around every corner. We get to take robots, put them through their paces, see what works, see what breaks, and then figure out how to make them better. For people who love building things, that’s a pretty incredible playground. There’s serious engineering behind it, but you still have those moments where you step back and think, “I can’t believe this is what we get to do for a living.”
